en: The Root Text of the *Śataśāstra* in One Volume,
composed by the Bodhisattva Āryadeva and translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.
Chapter One: Refuting Permanence All things arise as effects; Therefore, they possess the nature of impermanence.
Thus, none other than the Buddha Is rightly titled the Tathāgata.
There is no time, place, or thing that possesses an intrinsic nature not produced by conditions;
therefore, there is no time, place, or thing that possesses an intrinsic nature and is eternally abiding.
An intrinsic nature does not exist without a cause, and that which has a cause is not eternal.
Therefore, since there is no cause for its establishment, true vision declares it to be non-existent.
Seeing that which is produced as impermanent, one might claim that what is unproduced is permanent;
yet, having seen that the impermanent exists, one should say that the nature of permanence does not exist.
Fools engage in false conceptualization, claiming that emptiness and the like are permanent;
yet even the wise, relying upon the conventional world, do not perceive this meaning.
It is not that it exists only in a single part, nor does it pervade all parts.
Thus we know that each individual part possesses its own distinct whole.
If the substance of a phenomenon were truly existent, its functions of contraction and expansion could be perceived;
since this [substance] must necessarily arise from something else, it is established as a produced effect.
If separated from the fruit that is produced, there is no cause capable of producing;
therefore, all causes capable of producing become fruits that are produced.
All phenomena must undergo transformation before they can act as causes for further production.
How can such a cause of transformation be called eternal?
If that which was originally non-existent now exists, and nature (*svabhāva*) is taken as its eternal cause,
then since you admit the existence of nature, the [notion of] a cause is falsely established.
How can it be that based on a permanent nature, impermanence arises?
That cause and effect possess such different characteristics has never been seen in the world.
If one part were the cause while the remaining parts were not the cause;
It would then necessarily become manifold; because it is manifold, it is not eternal.
The subtle, spherical form that exists in the cause does not exist in the effect;
therefore, atoms do not combine through their entire substance.
Since it is not admitted that there is anything else within the location of a single atom,
one should likewise not admit that cause and effect are equal in dimension.
If an atom has an eastern side, it must necessarily have an eastern part.
If atoms possessed parts, how could they be "atoms"?
It is by taking up what is before and abandoning what is behind that one can speak of "motion.
If these two [aspects] do not exist, then motion itself should not exist.
The atom has no prior part, nor does it have middle or posterior parts;
thus, it cannot be seen by any eye whatsoever.
If the cause is destroyed by the effect, then that cause is not eternal.
Perhaps the fruit and the cause, though their two natures occupy different locations,
one never perceives any phenomenon that is both eternal and resistant;
therefore, that atoms are eternal has never been taught by the Buddhas.
Apart from the cause of that which binds and that which is bound, there is no further true liberation;
because the functions of production and maintenance are lacking, even if it were to exist, it would be called non-existent.
At the time of ultimate nirvāṇa, there are neither aggregates nor a self.
If one does not perceive nirvāṇa, upon what could nirvāṇa depend?
At that time, having abandoned all virtues, and being free from craving, what thought could there be?
If there were a self but no thought, it would simply be non-existent.
If there were a self remaining without remainder, then volition would certainly arise;
only when there is neither self nor volition do all states of existence cease to be.
If there were a self apart from suffering, then there would certainly be no nirvāṇa.
Therefore, within nirvāṇa, we are all eternally extinguished.
It is better to seek within the world than to seek in the ultimate truth;
for while there is little to be found in the world, in the ultimate truth there is nothing at all.
Chapter Two: Refuting the Self The internal self is truly neither male, Nor female, nor neither;
It is only due to ignorance That one refers to the self as a "person."
If, within the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), there is neither male, female, nor the non-dual;
how then can the characteristics of male and so forth arise from these primary elements?
You are "I" and others are "not-I"; therefore, the self has no fixed characteristic.
Is it not that one falsely discriminates a self within what is impermanent?
This self is identical to the body; as it is born again and again, it undergoes change.
Therefore, the principle that there exists a self apart from the body which is eternally abiding is untenable.
If a phenomenon is without contact, it is without movement;
therefore, the actions performed by the body cannot be created by a "life-principle" (jīva).
Since the self is eternally indestructible, why trouble oneself with the causes for its protection?
Who fears that the *vajra* will consume them, and grasps a staff to ward off the many woodworms?
If one harbors the notion of a past life, one then claims that the self is eternal;
yet if one sees the scars of former times, the body likewise ought to be eternally abiding.
If the self were to unite with volition and thereby become a thinker, then volition itself would not be volition; therefore, the self is not permanent.
If the self were to unite with pleasure and so forth, it would become manifold, just like pleasure and the rest.
Because the self is like pleasure and so forth, it is neither unitary nor eternal.
If one claims that the self is conscious and eternal, such a view is a false attachment brought about by auxiliary conditions;
it would be like claiming that fire is permanent and thus does not depend on fuel and the like.
Just as a moving object ceases to exist when it reaches its point of extinction, so too,
the notion of a self devoid of volition is logically untenable. Furthermore,
if a realm of volition were to arise in one location, that volition would be perceived in a different place.
Just as an iron bar melts away, my body should likewise perish.
When thought is small in measure like an atom, I am vast like space;
yet by observing only its own characteristic, one does not perceive thought.
If my merit were all-pervasive, why would others not receive it?
Since you claim that what can obstruct is omnipresent, it should not obstruct only one person.
If merit and compassionate intention were simultaneous, how could they produce all things?
He would be like one driven mad, utterly deluded and accomplishing nothing.
If one who possesses the skill to construct houses and other such things does not know how to enjoy them,
what could be more irrational than this?
That which has activity is impermanent; that which is empty and pervasive is without activity.
Since being useless is the same as having no intrinsic nature, why not rejoice in non-self?
Some contemplate the self as all-pervasive, while others see its measure as equal to the body.
Some maintain that [the self] is like an atom; the wise realize it does not exist.
A permanent phenomenon cannot be afflicted; how could one abandon affliction to attain liberation?
Therefore, to conceive of a permanent self and claim to have realized liberation is irrational.
If the self truly possessed an intrinsic nature, one should not praise the relinquishing of the self;
for if one were certain of its reality, the path toward liberation would be in vain.
If it does not exist within liberation, it likewise could not have existed previously.
That which is seen when there is no confusion should be known as its true nature.
If everything impermanent were simply annihilated, why would grass and such not be so?
If this principle were truly established, then even ignorance would not exist.
We directly perceive that formations such as form arise, abide, and cease from conditions;
therefore, know that the self you cling to, though it is asserted to exist, does not exist.
Just as sprouts and the like are produced by conditions, and seeds and the like arise through conditions.
Therefore, all impermanent phenomena arise from the impermanent;
because phenomena arise from conditions, their essence is not annihilated;
because phenomena cease due to conditions, their essence is likewise not eternal.
Chapter Three: Refuting Time If a jar and so forth exist in the future, they cannot simultaneously possess the past and present;
if the future possessed the past and present, it would follow that the future does not exist.
If the future has already passed away, yet possesses the essence of the future, then it would be eternally future; how could it become past or present?
If a dharma exists in the future, it must currently possess the characteristics of the future.
It ought to be the present; how then can it be called the future?
If the past and future exist just as the present does, why do they lack the functional capacity to grasp a fruit?
If their essence is eternally non-deficient, why are they not permanent?
If the past were already past, how could it be established as the past?
If the past were not past, how could it be established as the past?
If the future were already arising, how could it not be the present?
If there is no arising in the future, how can it not be eternal?
If there is no arising in the future and it is impermanent because of its destruction;
since there is no destruction in the past, why is it not called eternal?
The impermanence of the present world does not arise from the past and so forth;
apart from these two destinations, there is no third.
If the conditioned phenomena of a later birth already possessed a fixed essence beforehand, [they would be permanent].
To claim that there are persons with a fixed nature would not be a false attachment.
If a phenomenon arises from causes and conditions, it does not possess an intrinsic essence prior to its arising.
If something were to arise while already existing in essence, then once it has arisen, it would have to arise again.
If you see that the past and future exist, why do you not see their non-existence?
Since you see that the past and future exist, you should not say they are distant.
If unproduced phenomena existed, the cultivation of morality and so forth would be in vain.
If there is some slight action performed, the fruit does not pre-exist.
Since all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent, the fruit is not eternally present;
if it has a beginning and an end, the world universally agrees that it is not permanent.
Liberation would not require effort, for liberation has no coming or going;
yet if one were to allow for coming and going, then desire itself would be the one who is free from desire.
If one maintains that the fruit exists prior [to its cause], then one would be constructing palaces, houses, and ornaments [out of what already exists].
The pillars and so forth would be rendered useless;
likewise, it is the same for a fruit that did not previously exist.
That phenomena undergo transformation has never occurred among the wise.
Except for those who lack wisdom, who falsely discriminate and take it to be existent;
how could there be duration in impermanence?
If there is no duration, what essence could there be?
If there were abiding at the beginning, there should be no change or decay later.
Just as a single consciousness cannot cognize two objects,
so too a single object cannot be known by two consciousnesses.
If there were a time distinct from abiding, then abiding would not constitute that time;
if there were no time distinct from abiding, then subsequent cessation would not exist.
If the phenomenon (dharma) were different from impermanence, then the phenomenon would not be impermanent.
If phenomena and impermanence are one, then phenomena should have no abiding.
Since impermanence is initially weak, the power of abiding must surely be stronger;
for what reason, then, do these two later appear as a perversion?
If the power of impermanence were initially weak while pervading the essence of all phenomena,
then either nothing at all would endure, or everything would be eternal.
If impermanence were always present, then endurance would necessarily be eternally absent.
Either that phenomenon was originally eternal and later became non-eternal;
or, if a phenomenon were both impermanent and abiding simultaneously,
then its association with impermanence would be false, or its association with abiding would be empty.
Seeing nothing, one sees non-existence; turning the mind, it takes false objects as its condition.
Therefore, all is merely provisional; where there is recollection, we speak of "arising.
Chapter Four: Refuting Views One who receives the harmony [of the teaching] and yearns for supreme wisdom should be known as a vessel for the Dharma.
Apart from this, there would be no teacher or disciple, nor could one obtain the supreme benefit without a cause.
By teaching existence and its causes, as well as purity and the means to purity, the World-Honored One has provided guidance;
since worldly beings themselves do not understand, how could the fault lie with the Muni?
The abandonment of all existence for the sake of nirvāṇa is what is commonly accepted by all heterodox schools;
since the true emptiness [of our school] refutes everything, why would they not rejoice in it?
Not knowing the causes for abandonment and realization, they have no means by which to abandon or realize.
Therefore the Muni has said: "There is nothing else as cool and refreshing as this.
If one conceives doubt regarding the profound matters taught by the Buddha, one should rely upon signless emptiness and give rise to resolute faith."
Observing that the present still contains delusion, one knows that the future will surely be empty;
those who act in reliance upon such phenomena are deceived without end.
The wise person attains nirvana for themselves; this is what makes the difficult possible to do.
When a fool encounters a virtuous guide, he has no mind to follow him.
Not knowing [the truth], he feels no fear; yet even one of universal knowledge is likewise [free from fear].
It is only through partial knowledge that fear arises.
The laws of birth and death that flow with the current are constantly practiced by the foolish;
they have never cultivated the practice of flowing against the current, and for this reason they give rise to fear.
All those people who are deluded obstruct the true vision of others.
Without a basis for birth in the happy realms, how could one realize nirvāṇa?
It is better to violate the precepts than to damage right view;
through the precepts one is born in the happy realms, and through right view one attains nirvāṇa.
It would be better for one to give rise to the grasping of a self than to hold a view of emptiness and selflessness;
for the latter leads subsequently to the evil realms, while the former merely turns one away from nirvāṇa.
The sublime principle of emptiness and selflessness is the true realm of all Buddhas.
It can terrify all evil views; it is the non-dual gate to nirvāṇa.
When fools hear the name of the Dharma of emptiness, they all give rise to great fear;
like seeing one of great power, the timid and weak all flee in every direction.
Although the Buddhas have no [discursive] mind, they preach the Dharma that crushes the arguments of others;
yet those arguments collapse of their own accord, like wildfire consuming kindling.
All who awaken to the True Dharma will certainly take no pleasure in heterodox schools.
To eliminate other false paths, I have thus revealed the meaning of true emptiness.
If one understands the Buddha’s teaching on the principle of true emptiness and non-self,
one will not feel joy when things accord with it, nor will one feel aversion or fear when they conflict with it.
Seeing the multitudes of non-Buddhists, who for the most part pursue meaningless causes—
who would not feel deep compassion for those sentient beings who delight in the True Dharma?
Whether Brahmins, Nirgranthas, or the three schools of the Tathāgata;
The ear, eye, and mind can perceive it; therefore, the Buddha-dharma is profound and subtle.
That which is venerated by the Brahmins mostly incites deceit and fraud;
the teachings of the Nirgrantha heretics for the most part conform to ignorance.
They revere brahmins for the sake of reciting various mantras;
they take pity on the Nirgranthas because of their self-inflicted mortification of the body.
Yet such acts, being the result of painful karma, are not the cause of true liberation.
That which arises from superior physical action does not itself constitute the realization of liberation.
To summarize what the Buddha taught: it possesses two [features] that distinguish it from other schools;
by not harming living beings, one attains rebirth among gods or humans, and by contemplating emptiness, one realizes liberation.
The people of the world are addicted to their own schools, just as one loves one’s native land;
the True Dharma can crush them, and the factions of the heterodox take no joy in it.
Those with wisdom who seek superior virtue should believe in and accept the True Teaching.
The True Dharma is like the orb of the sun; those with eyes are able to see it because of it.
Chapter Five: Refuting the Sense Organs and Their Objects Among the various parts of a jar, it is only its visible form (*rūpa*) that can be seen.
To claim that the entire jar is visible—how could such a person realize the truth?
All those of superior wisdom, following the meaning previously explained,
should negate [the reality of] all categories of odor, flavor, and tangibility.
If one were to say that by seeing only the color of a jar, one sees the jar itself;
Since one does not perceive the fragrance and so forth, it should be called "not seeing the jar.
As for obstructed forms, their substance is not entirely visible;
their parts and the space between them are separated by those very parts.
One should carefully and thoroughly examine whether atoms possess parts or not;
to cite what is unestablished as proof will ultimately fail to establish the point.
All phenomena that possess resistance are composed of multiple constituent parts.
The same applies to words and letters; therefore, they are not apprehended by the sense faculties.
Since shape exists apart from manifest color, how can it be apprehended?
If shape is apprehended through manifest color, why is it not apprehended by the body faculty?
If there were a cause for form that was distinct from form itself, it should not be visible to the eye;
since the essences of these two things are different, why are they not perceived separately?
When the body perceives solidity and so forth, one conventionally establishes the names "earth" and so on.
Therefore, it is only within the context of tactile contact that the distinctions of earth and so forth are spoken of.
When a jar is perceived arising, no distinct quality (*guṇa*) is seen;
since its substance arises exactly as it is seen, its substantial nature (*dravyasvabhāva*) is entirely non-existent.
The eye and the other [faculties] are all composed of the great elements; why is it that the eye sees and not the others?
Therefore, the fruit of karma is inconceivable—this is the true teaching of the Muni.
Since the object of cognition does not yet exist, cognition does not precede the act of seeing.
If cognition were to follow later, it would be discarded; if they were simultaneous, one would see what is useless.
If the eye traveled to reach its object, the sight of distant forms should be delayed;
why then is it not equally clear when perceiving forms both extremely far and near?
If one acts only after having seen [the object], then acting would be useless;
if one goes without seeing it, there would certainly be no desire to see.
If one could observe without going, one should see all forms.
Since the eye has no movement, it is neither distant nor obstructed.
The essence, characteristics, and functions of all phenomena must necessarily remain the same before and after;
how then can this visual faculty not perceive its own nature?
In the eye there is no visual consciousness, and within visual consciousness there is no eye or form;
since both are absent within form, how can they combine to see form?
If that which is heard could express meaning, why would it not constitute non-sound?
If sound were not expressive, why would it give rise to understanding when perceived?
If sound is heard only upon reaching the ear, how can one comprehend the nature of that sound?
Since there is no principle for sound to be articulated all at once, how could it be known in its entirety?
Even that which is not heard ought not to be of the nature of sound;
for it is logically inconsistent that what was previously non-existent should later come to be.
If the mind were separate from the sense faculties, its departure [from the body] would likewise be useless.
If such a "life-principle" (jīva) were to exist, it would necessarily be eternally without mind.
It causes the mind to falsely grasp at sense-objects, relying on prior perceptions like a mirage to falsely establish the meanings of various phenomena;
this should be known as the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha).
With the eye, forms, and so forth as conditions, various consciousnesses arise like an illusion;
if one were to grasp them as truly existent, the analogy of an illusion would not hold.
Of all things that exist in the world, there is none that is not difficult to fathom.
The principles regarding the faculties and their objects are likewise; why should the wise be startled by this wonder!
All phenomena are like a whirling firebrand, like transformations, dreams, and illusions;
they are like the moon reflected in water, a comet, an echo, a mirage, and floating clouds.
Chapter Six: Refuting the Extremes If all phenomena were truly existent, they would not depend on others for their establishment;
since they necessarily depend on others for their establishment, it is certain that they are not truly existent.
The jar does not exist as identical to form, nor does the jar exist apart from form;
form does not exist dependent upon the jar, nor does the jar exist dependent upon form.
If one perceives these two characteristics as distinct, one claims that there is a "sameness" existing apart from the jar.
Since the two characteristics are distinct, they should exist separately from the jar;
if "one" is not called a jar, then the jar should not be called "one.
Since jar and one have never been joined, the jar should lack the name "one."
If form were pervasive throughout the substance, then form would have to be called "great";
if the opponent's argument is not [valid], then one should set forth the meaning of one's own school.
Since there are characteristics such as number and so forth, the characterized object cannot be established.
Apart from these, there is no other cause; therefore, all phenomena do not exist [as independent entities].
A jar does not exist apart from its distinct parts; therefore, the essence of the jar is not one.
Since each individual part is not the jar, the essence of the jar is also not many.
It is not that the substance of contact does not exist, yet it is conjoined with the substance of contact;
therefore, the various phenomena such as form cannot be combined to constitute a jar.
Form is but one part of the jar; therefore, the substance of form is not the jar.
Since the "whole" (avayavin) does not exist, how can the "part" (avayava) exist?
All things such as form (rūpa) are identical in their nature as form and so forth; there is no difference in their characteristics.
If only one instance of this class is a "vase," what is the reason that the others are not?
If form were distinct from taste and the rest, yet not distinct from the jar and the like;
and if the jar and the like were identical to taste and the rest, then how could form itself be the jar and the like?
Since the jar and the like would thus lack a cause, their substance could not achieve fruition.
Therefore, if [the pot] were distinct from color and so forth, the pot and such would certainly be non-existent.
If a cause for the pot and such existed, it could serve as the cause for the pot and such;
since a cause for the pot and such does not exist, how could the pot and such arise?
When form and the other [elements] are combined, they ultimately do not constitute fragrance and the like;
therefore, a single unified entity formed by combination must be non-existent, just as a jar and such are [non-existent].
Just as the substance of a jar is truly non-existent apart from form and the others, so it is here.
The substance of form should likewise be so; it does not exist apart from wind and the other elements.
Heat is itself the nature of fire; how could that which is not heat burn?
Therefore, the substance of fuel is non-existent, and apart from this, fire does not exist.
Since heat is established through its association with other [elements], why is it not fire?
If heat were not established by others, then the nature of fire would not exist.
If fire were subtle and lacked fuel, then fire should exist apart from fuel.
If fire were to possess even a subtle atom of fuel, there would have to be a subtle atom of fire;
yet when examining all phenomena closely, not a single entity exists as a reality.
Since a single entity does not exist, multiple entities likewise cannot exist.
If a phenomenon has nothing further remaining, you might claim it is a single entity;
yet all phenomena possess the three natures, and thus a single entity is non-existent.
Existence, non-existence, both, and neither—oneness and non-oneness are both extinguished.
They should be assigned accordingly; yet the wise realize they are not real.
Regarding the provisional phenomena of the continuum, they hold false views of them as truly permanent;
regarding the provisional phenomena of accumulation, they wrongly cling to them as being substantially existent.
All phenomena arise from a multitude of conditions; their nature is weak and lacks autonomy.
Being false and established in dependence upon others, therefore both "self" and "phenomena" are non-existent.
Effects are produced through the synthesis of many conditions; apart from these conditions, there is no separate effect.
Thus, the conjunction with a fruit—this the sages realize is entirely non-existent.
Consciousness is the seed of all existence, and the object is the sphere of consciousness;
when one perceives that objects are without self, the seeds of all existence are extinguished.
Chapter Seven: Refuting the Characteristics of the Conditioned If that which was originally non-existent arises, why does it not arise when it previously did not exist?
If that which already exists arises, then that which exists later should also arise.
If the effect could contradict its cause, it would be illogical for it not to exist beforehand;
if the effect were established, the cause would be useless, and if it existed beforehand, it could not be produced.
At this time there is no production, and at that time there is likewise no production.
Since this and that do not arise at any time, when could arising ever occur?
Just as the meaning of arising is non-existent in relation to self-nature, it is likewise so for other-nature;
how, then, could the meaning of arising be established as real?
If the three stages of beginning, middle, and end do not exist prior to their production, how can they be established?
Since two and one are non-existent, how can each one exist?
It is not produced apart from other-nature; it arises solely from self-nature.
Since it does not arise from another nor from both together, arising is certainly non-existent.
It cannot be said to exist either before, after, or simultaneously with the two;
therefore, arising, like the vase and so forth, exists only conventionally and not truly.
If the old were before the new, its prior arising would be illogical;
if the old were after the new, its subsequent arising could not be established.
The present does not arise by depending on the present, nor does it arise by depending on the past or the future.
The future does not arise from causes, nor do the past and present worlds originate [from them].
If they were fully present, there would be no coming; since they have already ceased, they should not be going.
Such is the nature and characteristic of phenomena; thus, metaphors such as illusions are not false.
The three characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing cannot exist simultaneously;
they are likewise non-existent sequentially. How can you insist that they exist?
If these characteristics such as arising were themselves to have further distinct characteristics of arising and so forth, [there would be an infinite regress].
Cessation should abide as it arises, or arising should abide as it ceases.
If the characterized were different from the characterizer, how could its essence not be impermanent?
If they were not different, the four [phases] would be identical, or else none would exist at all.
There is existence that does not give rise to existent dharmas; there is existence that does not give rise to non-existent dharmas.
There is non-existence that does not give rise to existent dharmas; there is non-existence that does not give rise to non-existent dharmas.
Existence does not constitute existent dharmas; existence does not constitute non-existent dharmas.
There is nothing that does not become an existent thing, nor anything that does not become a non-existent thing.
That which is half-born and half-unborn cannot be the essence of the time of birth;
otherwise, by virtue of being in the state of not yet born, it would also have to be the time of birth.
If the time of arising were itself the fruit, then its essence would not be the time of arising;
if the time of arising were self-existent, it would lose its nature as the time of arising.
Since that which has already arisen is different from that which has not yet arisen, there must be a distinct intermediate state between them.
The time of arising is distinct from the two other states; therefore, there must be a separate intermediate state.
If you claim that one attains the "already arisen" state only after relinquishing the "arising" state, then there must be something else present at the time of attainment that can be perceived.
If it has reached the state of having already arisen, logically there can be no time of arising;
if that which has already arisen were to have a time of arising, how could it originate from that?
If one posits a "time of arising" before it has reached the state of having already arisen; [then that too is untenable].
Why not say there is "no jar"?
Because there is no distinction [between the jar] prior to its arising.
It is not the case that at the time of arising it has a function capable of distinguishing itself from the time prior to its arising.
Nor is it that its essence is not yet complete, distinct from the stage already arisen.
At the preceding stage, when [the entity] was arising, it did not exist; only at the subsequent stage is it said to exist.
Since it simultaneously establishes the stage already arisen, this stage is therefore not non-existent.
Sometimes it is called "already arisen," and never is it called "not yet originated.
Apart from these positions of existence and non-existence, who else could claim there is a "time of arising"?
Those who maintain that there is no distinct result produced apart from its cause— [their position is untenable].
The arising and ceasing of transformation are both logically untenable.
(8) Chapter Eight: Admonishing Disciples Due to minor causes and conditions, one doubts emptiness and claims it is not empty;
based on the principles and teachings in the preceding chapters, this should be further refuted.
If that which speaks and that which is spoken were to exist, the principle of emptiness would be non-existent;
since all phenomena are established through dependent conditions, these three factors do not exist as substantial entities.
If there were the fault of speaking only of emptiness, then the meaning of non-emptiness would be established.
Since it has already been clarified that [the opponent's position] is not non-empty, the meaning of emptiness should be established first.
Those who wish to refute the positions of others must necessarily establish their own positions;
why take pleasure in discussing the faults of others while failing to establish one's own?
To refute the singularistic clinging, the provisional establishment [of emptiness] is posited as the thesis;
once the three other clingings of others have been eliminated, one’s own thesis likewise does not stand.
If clinging is admitted to be directly perceived, the reason for emptiness lacks probative power.
The reasons perceived by other schools are not accepted by this school.
If the principle of non-emptiness does not exist, how can the principle of emptiness be established?
Since you do not establish emptiness, non-emptiness likewise cannot be established.
If you admit the existence of the thesis of non-existence, then the thesis of existence can be established;
if the thesis of non-existence does not exist, then the thesis of existence cannot be established.
If all phenomena are empty, how can fire be called "hot"?
This has already been thoroughly refuted as before: fire and heat are conventional, not ultimate.
If you claim that phenomena truly exist, then emptiness is merely a negation of that claim;
in that case, all four philosophical systems would be ultimately true—seeing what fault do you have that you abandon them?
If all phenomena were entirely non-existent, then birth and death would not exist;
how could the Buddhas ever have permitted the grasping of phenomena as definitively non-existent?
If they truly transcend both existence and non-existence, for what reason do you say they exist conventionally?
Your own fundamental position is likewise so; what is the point of raising further objections?
If all phenomena were entirely non-existent, their distinctions could not exist;
yet if one clings to the view that all phenomena exist, their distinctions would likewise be non-existent.
If you claim that phenomena do not exist, there can be no cause capable of refuting existence;
since the cause for refuting existence has already been clarified, why do you not establish your own thesis?
To say that the cause for refutation is easily found is merely empty conventional talk.
For what reason are you unable to refute the meaning of "empty of intrinsic nature"?
The term "existent" designates that phenomena exist, implying that phenomena are truly not non-existent;
the term "non-existent" indicates that phenomena do not exist, implying that phenomena should truly not be existent.
Because one understands that phenomena exist through names, one consequently claims that phenomena are not non-existent;
because one knows that phenomena are non-existent through names, one should believe that phenomena are not existent.
All that can be spoken of in the world is merely conventional and not real.
Transcending worldly conventions and names, this is indeed the truth and not the false.
To slander all phenomena as non-existent may lead one to fall into the view of nihilism;
yet, since one merely eliminates all deluded attachments, how can it be said that one falls into nihilism?
Because existence is not truly existent, non-existence is also not truly nonexistent;
since there is no such thing as true nonexistence, how can there be true existence?
If existence is proven by means of the emptiness of phenomena, then the emptiness of phenomena itself should not be established.
Because the thesis and the reason are not distinct, the essence of the reason is in fact non-existent.
To claim that the example of emptiness exists separately, while using it to illustrate that all phenomena are not empty, would mean that only the example itself could be established;
it would be like asserting that the internal self is black simply because a crow is black.
If phenomena are empty by their very nature, what merit is there in seeing that emptiness?
The bonds of false conceptualization are severed upon realizing emptiness;
yet to see [emptiness] as a thing or a non-thing violates both the ultimate and the conventional truths.
Therefore, identity with existence and difference from it—both cannot be asserted.
Existence, non-existence, both, and neither—all such tenets are utterly quiescent;
should one wish to raise objections against them, they can ultimately never be sustained.
When the Bodhisattva Āryadeva had completed his treatise, he again set forth the refutation of heterodox views, further speaking in verse:
"I have acted as a torch for the fire that consumes false doctrines, Drenching them with the clarified butter of the Tathāgata’s true teaching, And fanning the vast wind of logic (hetuvidyā);
Who would dare cast themselves like a moth into such a fierce flame?"
The Root Text of the Extensive Hundred Treatise, One Fascicle.
